item.title: EventSpikeSeg: Memory-Aware Mixed-Signal Architecture for Event-Camera Spiking Segmentation
item.description: arXiv:2611.18524v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Event-camera segmentation requires persistent neural state despite sparse input events, making memory organization a central constraint on embedded implementation. We present EventSpikeSeg, a mixed-signal architecture combining resident capacitor memory with shared analog processing in GF180MCU 180-nm CMOS. Its 25-population spiking encoder-decoder has 143,824 synaptic weights but requires 30,976,000 membrane states at 440 x 640 resolution. The mapping specifies chronological 5-ms model updates, digital event/address services and 64-state capacitor banks. Characterization covers 22 module families and 74 operating points, distinguishing transistor simulations from digital-library estimates. Nominal results include 41.711 microwatts biased neuron-core power, 3.338-pJ positive terminal energy for a 1.4-microsecond cell read, and 0.531-mV selected-state drift over a 5-ms extracted-tile hold. Commit and coupling errors are reported separately. The software checkpoint records 27.976% mean intersection-over-union on a held-out six-class DSEC split; this is not hardware accuracy. Component layouts and simulation evidence quantify local implementation costs and expose storage replication and service scheduling as scaling constraints. A detailed SPICE-calibrated behavioral forward simulation of one full-resolution DSEC frame achieves 24.26% mean intersection-over-union, versus 26.22% for the matched PyTorch reference, using a compact 5-fF bank variant and external count/voltage calibration. Physical full-network operation, system energy and mismatch robustness remain unverified.
item.dc:creator: Amir Mohammad Khadem Hosseini, Sattar Mirzakuchaki

item.title: When No-Reference Image Quality Models Meet MAP Estimation in Diffusion Latents
item.description: arXiv:2403.06406v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Contemporary no-reference image quality assessment (NR-IQA) models can effectively quantify perceived image quality, often achieving strong correlations with human perceptual scores on standard IQA benchmarks. Yet, limited efforts have been devoted to treating NR-IQA models as natural image priors for real-world image enhancement, and consequently comparing them from a perceptual optimization standpoint. In this work, we show -- for the first time -- that NR-IQA models can be plugged into the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation framework for image enhancement. This is achieved by performing gradient ascent in the diffusion latent space rather than in the raw pixel domain, leveraging a pretrained differentiable and bijective diffusion process. Likely, different NR-IQA models lead to different enhanced outputs, which in turn provides a new computational means of comparing them. Unlike conventional correlation-based measures, our comparison method offers complementary insights into the respective strengths and weaknesses of the competing NR-IQA models in perceptual optimization scenarios. Additionally, we aim to improve the best-performing NR-IQA model in diffusion latent MAP estimation by incorporating the advantages of other top-performing methods. The resulting model delivers noticeably better results in enhancing real-world images afflicted by unknown and complex distortions, all preserving a high degree of image fidelity.
item.dc:creator: Weixia Zhang, Dingquan Li, Guangtao Zhai, Xiaokang Yang, Kede Ma

item.title: Evaluating the Generalizability and Explainability of Firn Image Classification with Topological Features
item.description: arXiv:2504.16150v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper we evaluate the performance of topological features for generalizable and explainable classification of firn image data, with the broader goal of understanding the advantages, pitfalls, and trade-offs in topological featurization. Firn refers to layers of granular snow within glaciers that haven't yet been compressed into ice. This compaction process imposes distinct topological and geometric structure on firn that varies with depth within the firn column. However, the limited and highly correlated training data available results in naive classifiers (such as convolutional neural networks) overfitting to orientation-dependent features. This motivates us to evaluate topological data analysis (TDA) as a way to design features which capture the shape of the firn data while retaining a large degree of invariance. We evaluate two classes of topological features, sublevel set features and distance transform features, together with persistence curves, to predict sample depth from firn images. A range of challenging training-test scenarios reveals that no one choice of method dominates in all categories. In particular, we see a tradeoff between accuracy on the one hand, and generalizability and explainability (via feature importance) on the other.
item.dc:creator: Jesse Dimino, Matt Jester, Kaitlin Keegan, Thomas Weighill, Sarah Day

item.title: BusterX++: Towards Unified Cross-Modal AI-Generated Content Detection and Explanation with MLLM
item.description: arXiv:2507.14632v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rapid advancement of generative AI has substantially improved image and video synthesis, amplifying the risk of multimodal visual misinformation. Recent MLLMs have shown promise for transparent AI-generated content detection through reasoning and explanation, yet existing approaches largely treat image and video forensics as isolated tasks, leaving cross-modal synergies underexplored. To address this, we present \textbf{BusterX++}, a unified MLLM for joint image and video detection with interpretable reasoning. We also introduce \textbf{GenBuster-Bench++}, a curated benchmark containing balanced image and video samples spanning recent generation models and diverse real-world scenarios, with synthetic images and videos screened using the same human difficulty criterion. Using this controlled setting, we revisit the widely adopted SFT+RL post-training paradigm. Notably, in the unified image-video setting, our results demonstrate that a single-stage pure RL strategy driven primarily by sparse outcome rewards outperforms a strong SFT+RL baseline. We observe that single-stage pure RL maintains higher policy entropy than SFT-initialized RL throughout training. This observation suggests a possible role for exploration in the performance gains observed under unified image-video training. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BusterX++ achieves state-of-the-art performance, highlighting the powerful potential of RL for unified cross-modal visual reasoning.
item.dc:creator: Haiquan Wen, Tianxiao Li, Zhenglin Huang, Yiwei He, Guangliang Cheng

item.title: Click, Predict, Trust: Clinician-Guided and Clinician-Evaluated AI Segmentation for Lung Cancer CT-Based Prognosis within the Knowledge-to-Action Framework
item.description: arXiv:2510.17039v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer mortality, with CT imaging central to screening, prognosis, and treatment. Manual segmentation is variable and time-intensive, while deep learning (DL) offers automation but faces barriers to clinical adoption. Guided by the Knowledge-to-Action framework, this study develops a clinician-in-the-loop DL pipeline to enhance reproducibility, prognostic accuracy, and clinical trust. Multi-center CT data from 999 patients across 12 public datasets were analyzed using five DL models (3D Attention U-Net, ResUNet, VNet, ReconNet, SAM-Med3D), benchmarked against expert contours on whole and click-point cropped images. Segmentation reproducibility was assessed using 497 PySERA-extracted radiomic features via Spearman correlation, ICC, Wilcoxon tests, and MANOVA, while prognostic modeling compared supervised (SL) and semi-supervised learning (SSL) across 38 dimensionality reduction strategies and 24 classifiers. Six physicians qualitatively evaluated masks across seven domains, including clinical meaningfulness, boundary quality, prognostic value, trust, and workflow integration. VNet achieved the best performance (Dice = 0.83, IoU = 0.71), radiomic stability (mean correlation = 0.76, ICC = 0.65), and predictive accuracy under SSL (accuracy = 0.88, F1 = 0.83). SSL consistently outperformed SL across models. Radiologists favored VNet for peritumoral representation and smoother boundaries, preferring AI-generated initial masks for refinement rather than replacement. These results demonstrate that integrating VNet with SSL yields accurate, reproducible, and clinically trusted CT-based lung cancer prognosis, highlighting a feasible path toward physician-centered AI translation.

item.title: LatentFM: A Latent Flow Matching Approach for Generative Medical Image Segmentation
item.description: arXiv:2512.04821v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative models have achieved remarkable progress with the emergence of flow matching (FM). It has demonstrated strong generative capabilities and attracted significant attention as a simulation-free flow-based framework capable of learning exact data densities. Motivated by these advances, we propose LatentFM, a flow-based model operating in the latent space for medical image segmentation. To model the data distribution, we first design two variational autoencoders (VAEs) to encode both medical images and their corresponding masks into a lower-dimensional latent space. We then estimate a conditional velocity field that guides the flow based on the input image. By sampling multiple latent representations, our method synthesizes diverse segmentation outputs whose pixel-wise variance reliably captures the underlying data distribution, enabling both highly accurate and uncertainty-aware predictions. Furthermore, we generate confidence maps that quantify the model certainty, providing clinicians with richer information for deeper analysis. We conduct experiments on two datasets, ISIC-2018 and CVC-Clinic, and compare our method with several prior baselines, including both deterministic and generative approach models. Through comprehensive evaluations, both qualitative and quantitative results show that our approach achieves superior segmentation accuracy while remaining highly efficient in the latent space.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the FISU Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence 2026 (FJCAI 2026), pp. 288-294, ISBN: 978-604-45-2586-0

item.title: Vision-language models lag human performance on physical dynamics and intent reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2601.01547v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Spatial intelligence is central to embodied cognition, yet contemporary AI systems still struggle to reason about physical interactions in open-world human environments. Despite strong performance on controlled benchmarks, vision-language models often fail to jointly model physical dynamics, reference frames, and the latent human intentions that drive spatial change. We introduce Teleo-Spatial Intelligence (TSI), which captures an important aspect of spatial reasoning: integrating physical dynamics and action goals to reason about actions and their spatial consequences. To evaluate TSI, we present EscherVerse, a large-scale open-world resource built from 11,328 real-world videos, including an 8,000-example benchmark and a 35,963-example instruction-tuning set. Across 27 state-of-the-art vision-language models and an independent analysis of first-pass human responses from 11 annotators, we identify a persistent teleo-spatial reasoning gap: the strongest proprietary model achieves 57.26% overall accuracy, far below first-pass human performance, which ranges from 84.81% to 95.14% with a mean of 90.62%. Fine-tuning on real-world, intent-aware data narrows this gap for open-weight models, but does not close it. EscherVerse provides a diagnostic testbed for purpose-aware spatial reasoning and highlights a critical gap between pattern recognition and human-level understanding in embodied AI.
item.dc:creator: Tianjun Gu, Jingyu Gong, Zhizhong Zhang, Yuan Xie, Lizhuang Ma, Xin Tan, Athanasios V. Vasilakos

item.title: ISLA: Ensemble learning and domain adaptation for generalizable acute ischemic stroke lesion segmentation in diffusion MRI with clinical validation
item.description: arXiv:2601.08732v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurate segmentation of acute ischemic stroke (AIS) lesions on MRI is essential for clinical decision-making. Deep learning methods offer a promising approach to automating this task. However, they often generalize poorly to unseen clinical sites, and few AIS lesion segmentation methods have been externally validated. In this study, we propose $\mathit{ISLA}$ (Ischemic Stroke Lesion Analyzer), a framework for AIS lesion segmentation built on the design principles of $\mathit{nnU\text{-}Net}$. $\mathit{ISLA}$ combines attention modules, deep supervision, and ensemble learning across different input resolutions, convolutional block types, and loss functions. We also introduce $\mathit{ISLA\text{-}MT}$, a variant that leverages unlabeled target-domain images through semi-supervised learning. We trained both approaches on the SOOP and ISLES 2022 datasets and evaluated on a held-out internal validation set of 253 cases, as well as on 590 cases from an independent multicenter clinical cohort. We compared them with three state-of-the-art pre-trained models and with $\mathit{nnU\text{-}Net}$ trained on the same data. $\mathit{ISLA}$ outperformed the pre-trained models on the internal validation set, while both $\mathit{ISLA}$ and $\mathit{ISLA\text{-}MT}$ outperformed them on the external cohort. Although $\mathit{nnU\text{-}Net}$ performed slightly better than $\mathit{ISLA}$ internally, both $\mathit{ISLA}$ variants demonstrated better generalization to the external cohort. Furthermore, $\mathit{ISLA\text{-}MT}$ significantly improved performance over $\mathit{ISLA}$ on the external cohort. The proposed models performed particularly well on low-contrast lesions, and qualitative error analyses suggested greater robustness to acquisition artifacts. Both models are fast ($\sim$ 5 s per case), and their code and weights are publicly available at https://github.com/RocaVincent/isla_segmentation.

item.title: Tracing 3D Anatomy in 2D Strokes: Can Projection-Derived Masks Replace 3D Segmentation for Cervical Spine Fracture Recognition?
item.description: arXiv:2601.15235v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cervical spine fractures require rapid and accurate diagnosis, yet automatic CT interpretation remains challenging as subtle injuries must be assessed across large 3D volumes. We ask whether full 3D vertebra segmentation is necessary for fracture recognition, or whether vertebra masks approximated from 2D projections preserve sufficient diagnostic context. In the proposed multi-stage pipeline, a YOLOv8 detector localizes the cervical spine from multi-view variance projections (3D mean Intersection over Union 94.45%). Multi-label vertebra segmentation is performed with a DenseNet121-Unet on energy-based sagittal and coronal projections (mean Dice 87.86%). The predicted 2D masks are back-projected and fused into approximate 3D masks per vertebra to extract volumes of interest from the original CT, which are analyzed by an ensemble of 2.5D spatio-sequential CNN-Transformer models. On the full RSNA 2022 cohort at native prevalence (2,019 patients, five-fold cross-validation), the pipeline yields vertebra-level and patient-level F1-scores of 68.15% and 82.28%, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 91.63% and 90.95%, and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) of 75.64% and 92.00%. With the classifier architecture fixed, replacing 3D-segmentation masks by projection-derived masks changed vertebra-level and patient-level AUPRC by +1.03 and +0.65 points, and the pipeline differed from the reproduced RSNA 2022 winning solution by -0.55 and +0.15 points. No AUPRC difference was statistically significant, and fold-wise 95% confidence intervals excluded vertebra-level losses larger than 1.46 and 2.81 points, respectively. Explainability and interobserver analyses examine reliability. Projection-based mask approximation is therefore a viable proxy for 3D vertebra segmentation in cervical fracture recognition.

item.title: Free-GVC: Toward Retraining-Free Extreme Generative Video Compression with Temporal Coherence
item.description: arXiv:2602.09868v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Building on recent advances in video generation, generative video compression has emerged as a new paradigm for achieving visually pleasing reconstructions. However, existing methods exhibit limited exploitation of temporal correlations, causing noticeable flicker and degraded temporal coherence at ultra-low bitrates. In this paper, we propose Free-GVC, a retraining-free generative video compression framework that reformulates video coding as latent trajectory compression guided by a video diffusion prior. Our method operates at the group-of-pictures (GOP) level, encoding video segments into a compact latent space and progressively compressing them along the diffusion trajectory. To ensure perceptually consistent reconstruction across GOPs, we introduce an Adaptive Quality Control module that dynamically constructs an online rate-perception surrogate model to predict the optimal diffusion step for each GOP. In addition, an Inter-GOP Alignment module establishes frame overlap and performs latent fusion between adjacent groups, thereby mitigating flicker and enhancing temporal coherence. Experiments show that Free-GVC achieves an average of 93.29% BD-Rate reduction in DISTS over the recent neural codec DCVC-RT, and a user study further confirms its superior perceptual quality and temporal coherence at ultra-low bitrates.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyue Ling, Chuqin Zhou, Chunyi Li, Yunuo Chen, Yuan Tian, Guo Lu, Wenjun Zhang

item.title: Comparative Analysis of 3D Convolutional and 2.5D Slice-Conditioned U-Net Architectures for MRI Super-Resolution via Elucidated Diffusion Models
item.description: arXiv:2603.14667v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) super-resolution (SR) methods that computationally enhance low-resolution acquisitions offer a software alternative to higher-field scanners. We study an elucidated diffusion model (EDM) framework for 2x in-plane brain MRI SR and compare two U-Net backbones: (i) a 3D convolutional U-Net that processes volumetric patches and (ii) a 2.5D slice-conditioned U-Net that super-resolves each slice while conditioning on its two neighbouring slices. All models are trained from scratch to convergence on 500 subjects of the NKI cohort of FOMO60K, with a separate 6-subject validation set for checkpoint selection, and evaluated on 70 held-out subjects with subject-level statistics against baselines (EDSR, Swin2SR, Res-SRDiff) trained on the same data. Neither architecture is better overall. On the degradation used in training the two are tied (37.72 dB PSNR for the 3D model and 37.70 dB for the 2.5D model), 0.2 dB ahead of EDSR. When the test degradation changes to k-space truncation, EDSR matches the diffusion models, and with added noise the 2.5D model is the most accurate method. When the test cohort changes to 70 subjects of an external dataset (IXI), the 3D model is the most accurate, 0.4 dB ahead of the best baseline and 0.9 dB ahead of the 2.5D model in foreground PSNR.
item.dc:creator: Hendrik Chiche, Eshaan Gulati, Ludovic Corcos, Logan Rouge

item.title: What DINO saw: ALiBi positional encoding reduces positional bias in Vision Transformers
item.description: arXiv:2603.16840v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) - especially feature foundation models like DINOv2 - learn rich representations useful for many downstream tasks. However, architectural choices (such as positional encoding) can lead to these models displaying positional biases and artefacts independent of semantic content. This makes zero-shot adaption difficult in fields like material science, where images are often cross-sections of homogeneous microstructure (i.e. having no preferred direction). In this work, we investigate the positional bias in ViTs via linear probing, finding it present across a range of objectives and positional encodings, and subsequently reduce it by finetuning models to use ALiBi relative positional encoding. We demonstrate that these models retain desirable general semantics and their unbiased features can be used successfully in trainable segmentation of complex microscopy images.

item.title: Open-Set Supervised 3D Anomaly Detection: An Industrial Dataset and a Generalisable Framework for Unknown Defects
item.description: arXiv:2604.01171v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Although self-supervised 3D anomaly detection assumes that acquiring high-precision point clouds is computationally expensive, in real manufacturing scenarios it is often feasible to collect a limited number of anomalous samples. Therefore, we study open-set supervised 3D anomaly detection, where the model is trained with only normal samples and a small number of known anomalous samples, aiming to identify unknown anomalies at test time. We present Open-Industry, a high-quality industrial dataset containing 20 categories, each with five real anomaly types collected from production lines. We first adapt general open-set anomaly detection methods to accommodate 3D point cloud inputs better. Building upon this, we propose Open3D-AD, a point-cloud-oriented approach that leverages normal samples, simulated anomalies, and partially observed real anomalies to model the probability density distributions of normal and anomalous data. Then, we introduce a simple Correspondence Distributions Subsampling to reduce the overlap between normal and non-normal distributions, enabling stronger dual distributions modeling. Based on these contributions, we establish a comprehensive benchmark and evaluate the proposed method extensively on Open-Industry as well as established datasets including Real3D-AD and Anomaly-ShapeNet. Benchmark results and ablation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of Open3D-AD and further reveal the potential of open-set supervised 3D anomaly detection.
item.dc:creator: Hanzhe Liang, Luocheng Zhang, Junyang Xia, HanLiang Zhou, Bingyang Guo, Yingxi Xie, Can Gao, Ruiyun Yu, Jinbao Wang, Pan Li

item.title: Where to Focus: Query-Modulated Multimodal Keyframe Selection for Long Video Understanding
item.description: arXiv:2604.17422v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long video understanding remains a formidable challenge for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) due to the prohibitive cost of processing dense frame sequences. Prevailing keyframe-selection methods rely on either a single visual-centric metric (e.g., CLIP similarity) or a static fusion of heuristic scores. This "one-size-fits-all" paradigm frequently fails: visual-only metrics are ineffective for plot-driven narrative queries, while indiscriminately adding textual scores introduces severe "modal noise" for purely visual tasks. To break this bottleneck, we propose Q-Gate, a plug-and-play, training-free framework that treats keyframe selection as a dynamic modality routing problem. We decouple retrieval into three lightweight expert streams: Visual Grounding for local details, Global Matching for scene semantics, and Contextual Alignment for subtitle-driven narratives. Crucially, Q-Gate introduces a Query-Modulated Gating Mechanism that uses the in-context reasoning of an LLM to assess query intent and dynamically allocate weights across the experts, activating necessary modalities while "muting" irrelevant ones to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio. Extensive experiments on LongVideoBench and Video-MME across multiple MLLM backbones show that Q-Gate outperforms representative keyframe-selection baselines in most settings, with particularly strong gains on long and medium videos, providing a robust and interpretable solution for scalable video reasoning. Code is available at https://github.com/shaoguangwang/Q_Gate

item.title: Directional Confusions Reveal Divergent Inductive Biases Through Rate-Distortion Geometry in Human and Machine Vision
item.description: arXiv:2604.21909v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Humans and modern vision models can reach similar classification accuracy while making systematically different kinds of mistakes -- differing not in how often they err, but in who gets mistaken for whom and in which direction. We show that these directional confusions reveal distinct inductive biases that are invisible to accuracy alone. Using matched human and deep vision model responses on a natural-image categorization task under 12 perturbation types, we quantify asymmetry in confusion matrices and link it to the shape of the information-error trade-off. We characterize this trade-off geometry using three signatures extracted from the rate-distortion (RD) frontier: slope beta, curvature kappa and efficiency (AUC). We find that humans exhibit broad but weak asymmetries, whereas deep vision models show sparser, stronger directional collapses. Robustness training reduces global asymmetry but fails to recover the human-like breadth-strength profile of graded similarity. Mechanistic simulations further show that different asymmetry organizations shift the RD frontier in opposite directions, even when matched for performance. Together, these results position directional confusions and RD geometry as compact, interpretable signatures of inductive bias under distribution shift.
item.dc:creator: Leyla Roksan Caglar, Pedro A. M. Mediano, Baihan Lin

item.title: Exposing and Mitigating Temporal Attack in Deepfake Video Detection
item.description: arXiv:2605.07398v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While spatiotemporal deepfake detectors achieve high AUC, our experiments reveal their susceptibility to evasion attacks. These models tend to overfit on fragile temporal spectrum cues, rather than learning robust semantic causality. To mitigate this vulnerability, we propose SpInShield, a temporal spectral-invariant defense framework explicitly designed to decouple semantic motion from manipulatable spectral artifacts. We propose a learnable spectral adversary that dynamically synthesizes severe spectral deformations, simulating extreme attack scenarios. By employing a shortcut suppression optimization strategy, SpInShield compels the encoder to extract reliable forensic cues while purging unstable spectral statistics from the latent space. Experiments show that SpInShield obtains competitive performance on widely used datasets and outperforms the strongest baseline by 21.30 percentage points in AUC under simulated amplitude spectral attacks.
item.dc:creator: Zheyuan Gu, Minghao Shao, Zhen Wang, Keyu Mao, Ailiang Lin, Mingyou Liang, Mingkun Xu, Shijie Zhang, Hao Jiang, Yusong Wang

item.title: InsHuman: Towards Natural and Identity-Preserving Human Insertion
item.description: arXiv:2605.07402v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Human insertion aims to naturally place specific individuals into a target background. Although existing image editing models may have such ability, they often produce failure cases, including inappropriate human pose in new background, inconsistent number of people, and modified facial identity. Moreover, publicly available human datasets often lack full-body portraits and realistic physical interaction between humans and their background. To address these challenges, we propose InsHuman for natural and identity-preserving human insertion. Specifically, we propose Human-Background Adaptive Fusion (HBAF), which detects foreground humans to obtain a binary mask and applies region-aware weighting to align the human regions between predicted and ground-truth latents, ensuring the person's pose, count, and overall appearance are coherently adapted to the target background.We further propose Face-to-Face ID-Preserving (FFIP), which detects and matches faces between the generated image and the source image in terms of face recognition features to enforce identity consistency for each face.In addition, we propose Bidirectional Data Pairing (BDP) strategy to construct BDP-InsHuman, a high-quality dataset with realistic human-background interactions. Experiments demonstrate that InsHuman achieves significant improvements in generating plausible images while keeping human identity unchanged.
item.dc:creator: Jie Li, Shulian Zhang, Wenbo Li, Jian Chen, Yong Guo

item.title: EdgeZSAD: Value-Range Quantization for Deploying Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection on Edge Neural Processing Units
item.description: arXiv:2606.16119v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantizing zero-shot industrial anomaly detectors for edge neural processing units can degrade defect detection and localization. We present EdgeZSAD (Edge Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection), a deployment framework whose methodological contribution is Value-Range Quantization (VRQ). We diagnose how attention Value tensors inherit overly wide ranges from fused query-key-value projections and assign independent ranges calibrated on source data, without retraining or changing quantized weights. The engineering application is native deployment of a foundation-model detector for industrial inspection, evaluated on three public benchmarks and Qualcomm edge devices. Under minimum-maximum and mean-squared-error calibration, VRQ improves image-level discrimination and per-region overlap. In the primary calibration set, it recovers 90-98% of the loss in combined image and pixel discrimination relative to half precision, with a small increase in latency over baseline quantization. Matched tensor overrides reproduce the recovery without adding graph nodes, identifying independent Value-range assignment as the effective intervention in the evaluated runtime family.
item.dc:creator: Taewan Cho, Seungmin Lee, Jiho Seo, Andrew Jaeyong Choi

item.title: When Simpler Is Better: Evaluating Translation Pipelines for Medieval Latin Manuscripts
item.description: arXiv:2607.03836v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite remarkable progress in machine translation, Vision Language Models (VLMs) struggle on historical manuscripts, a domain that stresses core Natural Language Processing (NLP) capabilities: low-resource transliteration, archaic vocabulary, and noisy input signals. We present a systematic framework for evaluating the full image-to-translation pipeline on medieval Latin manuscripts, a setting in which scribal shorthand, ligatures, and parchment degradation expose failure modes that are invisible in clean-text benchmarks. Benchmarking on the CATMuS Latin dataset reveals a specialization gap: domain-specific Optical Character Recognition (OCR) models reduce character error rate by up to 4.3$\times$ compared to general-purpose VLMs, despite operating at orders of magnitude fewer parameters. We introduce the Interpres-Parallel-Corpus (IPC), a novel dataset comprising 1,383 aligned manuscript image lines, transcriptions, and expert translations, to our knowledge the first of its kind for medieval Latin. Our experiments uncover a complexity paradox: the simplest pipeline, a specialized OCR model feeding directly into a VLM, outperforms all multi-component variants. Adding retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or post-OCR correction introduces prompt saturation and error propagation that degrade aggregate translation quality. These findings offer both a new benchmark and practical guidance for deploying translation systems in low-resource historical settings.
item.dc:creator: Nguyen Kim Hai Bui, Md. Easin Arafat, Tam\'as G\'abor Orosz, Mufti Mahmud

item.title: RFMSR: Residual Flow Matching for Image Super-Resolution
item.description: arXiv:2607.12753v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative image super-resolution (ISR) methods typically sample from a standard Gaussian prior and transport the sample to the data distribution, where the low-quality (LQ) input serves only as an external condition. However, the LQ image already carries rich structural information about the target high-quality (HQ) image, which makes a distribution approximating the LQ image a more suitable starting point, an idea that has been validated by a series of diffusion-based restoration methods. In contrast, recent flow-matching-based ISR methods still adopt the standard Gaussian prior and thereby discard such structural priors; moreover, existing single-step acceleration techniques, such as distillation and consistency training, either depend on an additional teacher or sacrifice the model's multi-step inference capability. In this paper, we propose Residual Flow Matching for Image Super-Resolution (RFMSR), which defines the source distribution as a Gaussian centered at the LQ latent, so that the flow starts from the LQ image rather than from pure noise and preserves the structural priors already present in the input. To achieve high-quality single-step generation, we further propose a simple yet effective training strategy that combines the supervision loss on the single-step output with the conditional flow matching (CFM) loss, enabling high-quality restoration with an arbitrary number of steps without resorting to distillation or other acceleration techniques. Extensive experiments show that RFMSR achieves competitive results against state-of-the-art methods. The source code is available at https://github.com/Faze-Hsw/RFMSR.
item.dc:creator: Shuwei Huang, Tianyao Luo, Jicheng Liu

item.title: The Second LoViF 2026 Challenge on Real-World All-in-One Image Restoration: Methods and Results
item.description: arXiv:2607.21118v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper presents a review of the second LoViF Challenge on Real-World All-in-One Image Restoration. The challenge aims to advance unified image restoration under diverse real-world degradation conditions, including blur, low-light, haze, rain, and snow. It provides a common benchmark for evaluating the restoration accuracy, robustness, and generalization capability of models across multiple degradation categories within a unified framework. The competition attracted 158 registered participants, and 20 teams were included in the final ranking after their submitted results were successfully reproduced and verified. This report provides a comprehensive analysis of the submitted solutions and corresponding results, highlighting recent advances in real-world all-in-one image restoration. The summarized methods and empirical findings reveal effective design strategies and establish an updated benchmark for future research in real-world low-level vision.

item.title: Projection Pursuit CPCANet for Domain Generalization
item.description: arXiv:2607.22117v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Domain Generalization (DG) aims to learn representations robust to distribution shifts. Recent geometric alignment methods, such as CPCANet, extract domain-invariant structures through batch-wise Common Principal Component Analysis (CPCA). However, CPCANet suffers from rank-deficient covariance estimation due to the small-sample-size issue in mini-batch training. To address this limitation, we propose Projection Pursuit CPCANet (PP-CPCANet), a covariance-free framework that learns a global orthogonal basis on the Stiefel manifold and jointly optimizes it with network parameters via the Cayley transform. We further introduce a symmetry-breaking detached-median PP dispersion objective to extract common principal components (CPCs) with dense and robust optimization signals. Experiments on four DG benchmarks show that PP-CPCANet achieves SOTA performance while maintaining stable training.
item.dc:creator: Yu-Hsi Chen, Abd-Krim Seghouane

item.title: AnaDiffusion: Anatomically Compositional Latent Diffusion for Controllable 3D Brain MRI Generation
item.description: arXiv:2608.23014v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: 3D brain MRI generation has made significant advances in medical imaging, simulation, and controllable anatomical analysis. However, existing generative models typically synthesize 3D volumes monolithically, often overlooking regional anatomical structures and limiting local controllability. To address these limitations, we introduce AnaDiffusion, an anatomically compositional latent diffusion framework that factorizes the generation process into distinct, anatomically meaningful regions, followed by part-to-whole assembly and global refinement. Our approach first trains part diffusion models to capture local structural priors. We then inject an assembled anatomical composite of the parts into the whole-brain latent representation and continue denoising. This mechanism enables the model to resolve global context while preserving the injected anatomy. AnaDiffusion thus produces explicit part assets and a globally coherent volume, enabling controllable part editing without subject-specific dense segmentation maps at inference. On a subject-disjoint ADNI test split, AnaDiffusion attains the lowest mean Fr\'echet distance (FID) in every evaluated region. In localized editing, it achieves substantially higher target transfer (paired MS-SSIM) than a segmentation-conditioned baseline, with off-target preservation close to the baseline's.
item.dc:creator: Huiwen Han, Lulin Liu, Bangya Liu, Yuanhao Cai, Nuo Chen, Xiaoqing Wang, Ziqian Xie, Chenyu You, Shuiwang Ji, Degui Zhi, Zhiwen Fan

item.title: UltraBench 2: Towards Robust Evaluation of Vision Foundation Models on Ultrasound
item.description: arXiv:2609.28610v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Benchmarking is an increasingly critical part of research in machine learning and the domains where it is applied, including healthcare. Yet, despite the steady development of new ultrasound foundation models in recent years, the development of well-designed benchmarks to evaluate them has lagged behind. This deficiency has led to fragmented and inconsistent evaluations of competing models, making it difficult to measure progress. To address this issue, we introduce UltraBench 2, a comprehensive benchmark with wide anatomical and task coverage, and a focus on standardization, reproducibility, and ease-of-use. Using this benchmark, we compare existing vision foundation models for ultrasound image analysis. Our analyses demonstrate that ultrasound-specific pretraining still leads on classification, but that state-of-the-art general-purpose models have drawn level on segmentation.
item.dc:creator: Ashwath Radhachandran, Adam Tupper, Christian Gagn\'e, William Speier

item.title: The Alignment Illusion in Multimodal Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2609.30210v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Layer-wise visual-text similarity in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) is widely interpreted as evidence that the language model progressively integrates visual content into a shared representation space. This reading rests on the assumption that scalar alignment scores reflect content-level cross-modal interaction. To test this assumption, we apply controlled interventions to the visual stream. Across 13 MLLMs from five families spanning 0.5B to 72B parameters, replacing projector-output visual tokens with Gaussian noise sharply reduces task accuracy, yet four standard scalar measures (CKA, SVCCA, MIR, and the leading principal-angle cosine) fail to consistently separate the corrupted stream from the original. We call this failure the alignment illusion and trace it to the shared language-model pathway: anisotropic MLP down-projections pull visual and text tokens toward common output directions, producing weight-induced alignment. We introduce the principal-angle gap (PA gap), defined as the difference between the top two principal-angle cosines, to distinguish leading-direction dominance from the broader overlap observed with structured visual content. Under graded visual corruption, the PA gap tracks task accuracy more consistently than the scalar scores we consider; under a structured but irrelevant image, it further exposes regimes in which internal geometry and task accuracy come apart. Internal visual-text alignment in MLLMs is therefore best read as a geometric diagnostic of the visual stream inside the language model rather than a direct proxy for content-level cross-modal interaction, and is most informative when calibrated by controlled task evidence.
item.dc:creator: Hong-Han Wang, Yuntao Wang, Hu Ding

item.title: Mind the RefGAP: Correcting Reference Attention in Diffusion-Based Visual Editing
item.description: arXiv:2609.35708v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reference-guided diffusion editors struggle to faithfully reproduce user-provided references. We observe that many diffusion editors allocate limited attention to the reference. For example, in LoomVideo, edit-region queries assign less than 1% of their attention mass to the reference. We introduce RefGAP, a training-free correction that determines logit-offset magnitudes online at each layer from the reference-attention mass measured during the forward pass. Positive offsets to reference logits strengthen reference usage by edit-region queries, while negative offsets for keep-region queries limit reference-induced changes outside the edit. Two global coefficients control the correction; they are selected once on validation data from four development diffusion editors and held fixed. Across seven diffusion-based image/video editors, RefGAP improves identity fidelity in head swapping and face swapping, where identity takes priority; on some editors this raises pose error, which delaying the correction reduces. RefGAP achieves a fidelity-preservation trade-off comparable to separately tuned constant edit-side biases, without per-approach strength sweeps. Additional experiments on virtual try-on and background replacement evaluate transfer beyond identity editing.
item.dc:creator: Yanan Wang, Shengcai Liao, Guangyi Liu, Xiaodan Liang

item.title: Synthetic Image Oversampling for Rare-Class Representation Learning in Deep Facial Phenotyping
item.description: arXiv:2610.23730v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent deep facial phenotyping methods can support the recognition of genetic syndromes, but patient images are often scarce and unevenly distributed across disorders. Synthetic facial images offer a way to supplement the training data without collecting additional patient photographs. Their usefulness, however, depends on whether they improve recognition of real patients: generated images may introduce artifacts or repeat features already represented in the training set. It is therefore necessary to examine both how much synthetic augmentation to use and which disorders benefit. We investigate disease-specific synthetic oversampling using images from the Phenotypic Disease Image Database to augment a subset of the GestaltMatcher Database. We compare increasing augmentation levels in an image-based model, GestaltMatcher-Arc, and a multimodal model, GestaltMML, while keeping the real training and patient-disjoint evaluation partitions fixed. Repeated training runs assess overall and disease-specific accuracy, and an exploratory embedding analysis examines changes in class compactness and separation. Augmentation improves mean recognition accuracy in both training setups, although gains remain modest in GestaltMatcher-Arc and continue across the tested levels in GestaltMML. These aggregate improvements are accompanied by uneven disease-level responses, including reduced accuracy for some disorders. In the embedding analysis, disorders with fewer real training images tend to gain more class separation, but geometric changes do not consistently track classification performance. Together, the findings support synthetic oversampling for limited-data facial phenotyping and emphasize the need to assess its amount and benefit for individual disorders within each training setup.
item.dc:creator: Miles Liao, Zhanliang Wang, Hongzhuo Chen, Kai Wang

item.title: Brain2Vec: A Self-Supervised 3D Foundation Model for Structural Brain MRI
item.description: arXiv:2610.28411v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deep learning models have become essential tools in medical imaging, yet training them end-to-end for diverse tasks remains challenging due to limited labeled data and computational constraints. To address this, we introduce Brain2Vec, a foundation model pre-trained on 74,425 T1-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans pooled from multiple studies. Brain2Vec can serve both as a weight initialization backbone for fine-tuning downstream tasks and as a standalone feature extractor. We evaluated Brain2Vec in three tasks: downstream predictive performance, convergence speed, and embedding quality. Using Brain2Vec's pretrained weights as initialization and fine-tuning on labeled data for a brain age prediction task, results demonstrate improved final accuracy and faster convergence compared to random initialization. Additionally, its frozen embeddings outperform anatomically defined volumetric features on four of five downstream classification tasks and perform competitively with a state-of-the-art foundation model pre-trained on substantially more data. On the independent BrainFMBench benchmark, Brain2Vec ranked first among six pretrained brain MRI foundation models on 9 of 15 sex, age, and BMI prediction tasks across five cohorts. Lastly, we show that Brain2Vec encodes information primarily from a spatially localized and neuroanatomically meaningful set of brain regions, and that manipulating a subset of latent features produces monotonic, region-specific effects on the reconstructed anatomy. Brain2Vec code and trained models are available as an open-source package on https://github.com/CBICA/Brain2Vec. Users can apply Brain2Vec locally by installing the package, or directly through the NiChart cloud platform https://cloud.neuroimagingchart.com, where Brain2Vec features can be derived without requiring local installation or specialized infrastructure.
item.dc:creator: Spiros Maggioros, Guray Erus, Gareth Harman, George Aidinis, Alexander Getka, Aristeidis Sotiras, Christos Davatzikos

item.title: Zoom Where the Answer Looks: Cross-Resolution Self-Distillation for MLLMs under Visual-Token Budgets
item.description: arXiv:2610.32664v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Under the small per-view visual-token budgets of efficient deployment, the fine text of documents, charts and infographics becomes illegible to multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Zooming in recovers it, but the region must be chosen before the model answers. Existing methods decode an answer or a box first, at the cost of generation, or read the attention available before answering, which localizes the evidence only in top layers whose depth varies with model size. Learned region proposers instead distill the attention of the model's answers, but on the same budgeted view. Yet this attention is precise only on a view the model can read: on Qwen3-VL-4B, a window around its peak covers 83% of the evidence on a high-resolution view but 54% on the budgeted view. Since answers and high-resolution views are available during training, we introduce LookZoom, a zooming method that trains a dedicated look token by cross-resolution self-distillation of the answer's attention: with the MLLM frozen, the token learns to attend on the budgeted view, before any answer, where the model's own correct answers attend on a high-resolution view. The region around its attention peak is the window to zoom into, and reinforcement learning then trains the MLLM to answer from both views. With 98 visual tokens per view on five text-rich benchmarks, LookZoom surpasses attention-guided zooming by 20-24 points and grounding-based zooming and learned crop routing by 12-15 points on Qwen3-VL at three scales, and it outperforms learned region proposers at every budget from 98 to 392 tokens. On Qwen3-VL, the look token alone, with the MLLM frozen, already surpasses every baseline that leaves the language model unchanged, and the recipe carries over to InternVL3.5 and Qwen2.5-VL.
item.dc:creator: Zhensheng Hu, Guanglong Xu, Guanqiang Hu

item.title: TAP-Out: Tracking Any Point in 360{\deg} via Outpainting
item.description: arXiv:2611.00406v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tracking points that leave the camera's field of view (FoV) requires reasoning about unobserved scene dynamics, a fundamentally different problem from tracking visible correspondences. We present TAP-Out, an offline method that makes this out-of-view (OOV) reasoning explicit by leveraging generative video outpainting as a world-model prior. Given a narrow-FoV input video, TAP-Out outpaints a complete 360{\deg} equirectangular video, locates target objects within the panoramic scene via video object segmentation, and synthesises object-centred perspective crops on which standard in-frame trackers operate. This decoupled design composes off-the-shelf foundation models without requiring task-specific architectural modifications. On the TAPVid360 benchmark, TAP-Out achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving OOV tracking accuracy by approximately 3x over the best prior method. We demonstrate its flexibility on out-of-frame object segmentation and detection and we provide detailed diagnostic analyses across motion regimes, static versus dynamic content, and hallucination quality, characterising when and why the approach succeeds or fails. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/finlay-hudson/TAP-Out
item.dc:creator: Finlay G. C. Hudson, James A. D. Gardner, William A. P. Smith

item.title: Real-VAS: a Real-World Video Amodal Segmentation Dataset
item.description: arXiv:2611.00430v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Amodal video object segmentation is fundamentally limited by the absence of datasets that combine real-world complexity with precise ground-truth annotations. To address this, we present Real Video Amodal Segmentation (Real-VAS), a new large-scale, zero-shot evaluation dataset built from composited real-image video. We introduce a novel data generation pipeline that enables the creation of programmatically consistent amodal ground truth for real-world footage, in which the object mask, occlusion boundary, and composited image are all derived from a single unoccluded source, without relying on human estimation or expensive 3D reconstruction. Our dataset is structured into two challenging scenarios: dynamic Occlusion, created by compositing two clips of moving objects, and a unique Container category featuring complex, physically constrained interactions. These container scenarios--On Surface Containment, Articulated Containment, and Mobile Containment--allow us to generate precise ground truth by simulating an object's motion based on its container's tracked transformation. As a result, Real-VAS provides a diverse and challenging benchmark for evaluating amodal segmentation models on realistic video with the precision of synthetic data. The dataset and generation code are publicly available at https://finlay-hudson.github.io/real_vas
item.dc:creator: Finlay G. C. Hudson, William A. P. Smith

item.title: A Straight Line Is Not a Camera Pose: Auditing Short-Clip Pose Benchmarks
item.description: arXiv:2611.00482v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many vision benchmarks align a prediction to the ground truth before scoring it. If the alignment minimises the error, an input-free template scores the truth's distance from everything the alignment can reach, so the ground truth alone fixes how well a template can score, before any model runs. Camera pose is our central case. The absolute trajectory error (ATE), the standard camera-motion measure, aligns camera positions by a similarity transform. On the common Sintel protocol, an image-free constant-velocity line has a lower mean ATE than 10 of 11 recent models and 85 of 110 published methods, and on Lightspeed than 5 of 9 models and 10 of 11 published methods. The straightness of the true paths separates these two from TUM, ScanNet, DyCheck and ADT, where every model beats the line. A residual signal-to-noise criterion with the alignment's first-order refit predicts when straightening a prediction lowers ATE in all but one of 4010 model-clip evaluations, including all 504 on three benchmarks registered in advance. The alignment also ignores where cameras look: rotating a trajectory by 30 degrees against its orientations leaves ATE unchanged yet worsens the static-point reprojection of every model on Sintel, TUM and ScanNet. Fitting the alignment's rotation to the predicted orientations gives pose-anchored ATE (PA-ATE), a one-function change at about ATE's cost (37 vs. 34 microseconds per clip). It is never below ATE, ranks every image-free reference below every model on Sintel, tracks the reprojection error under controlled rotation and straightening, largely preserves the models' order, and exposes Lightspeed ground-truth orientations that the images contradict. Beyond poses, templates beat some published methods on KITTI video depth, SSP-3D body shape and NoW faces, and in video depth this distance sets KITTI apart from Sintel and Bonn.
item.dc:creator: Xinyi Shi

item.title: Geometric Refinement and Distributional Alignment for Sim2Real Roadside LiDAR Detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.03936v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. We predicted our final score to four decimal places prior to submission. We report negative results at equal length, and give a full account of data provenance and compliance in Section 8, including a full account of every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
item.dc:creator: Aman Upganlawar

item.title: Coordinate Frame Recovery, Per Class NMS and Null Return Modelling for Sim2Real V2X LiDAR Detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.03940v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We describe our approach to the V2X-Real track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR from an Ouster OS1-64 unit, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.7457 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.4382 and a realism score of 0.9251. Three findings account for most of our result, and all three were diagnostic rather than architectural. First, a coordinate frame mismatch between our predictions and the evaluation ground truth was suppressing detection AP entirely; recovering it took our score from 0.3520 to 0.5147 in a single submission. Second, a single global non maximum suppression threshold was destroying genuine pedestrian detections, because pedestrians occur in groups and a 0.3 IoU threshold applied to a 0.7 m box suppresses distinct neighbouring people; correcting this per class raised overall mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295. Third, approximately 31 percent of the real reference point cloud consists of null returns encoded as the literal point (0, 0, 0), a format feature entirely absent from our synthetic clouds, which pinned Earth Mover's Distance near its floor until we modelled it. Negative results are reported at equal length, and Section 9 gives a full account of data provenance and compliance. That section also accounts for every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
item.dc:creator: Aman Upganlawar

item.title: Mamba3R: Fixed-Capacity Selective State Memory for Long-Sequence 3D Reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2611.04221v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Streaming 3D reconstruction must maintain geometric quality over long inputs within a fixed GPU budget. A pretrained recurrent model provides bounded state, but freezing its backbone also fixes its learned state-observation interactions. We introduce Mamba3R, a jointly designed state-memory adapter that provides a trainable adaptation path without updating the backbone or task heads. A selective state-space mixer jointly transforms native state features and a fixed-capacity auxiliary memory, explicit read and write paths carry information across frames, and a decomposed feedback path regulates what the added memory feeds back. Only 1.28 million adapter parameters are trained. Under a shared periodic-reset protocol, it lowers trajectory error and improves accumulated surface and depth accuracy over recurrent baselines on public indoor and outdoor datasets and robot-recorded traversals, gaining up to 40 percent on one metric. Matched comparisons support both the choice of the mixing operator and the utility of carrying the auxiliary memory across frames. Allocated memory remains unchanged and throughput moves by at most 1.4 percent from one to two thousand frames. Replaying its recorded traversals offline, the platform's RTX 4060 averages 11.7 frames per second within 5.1 GiB with the same checkpoint, a mean throughput covering the 10 Hz sensor rate.
item.dc:creator: Zhenxiang Xiong, Tianchen Deng, Nailin Wang, Lei Zhao, Guole Shen, Weidong Chen

item.title: TAQ-MOTR: Tracking-Aware Detection Query Formation for End-to-End Multiple Object Tracking
item.description: arXiv:2611.05205v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tracking-by-propagation (TBP) methods perform end-to-end multi-object tracking by propagating track queries across frames, jointly handling detection and identity association without heuristic post-processing while naturally modeling temporal information. However, as detection and association are tightly coupled, detection queries in TBP are expected to discover currently untracked objects and provide complementary current-frame evidence for challenging tracks whose queries and identities are retained. Existing methods largely inherit detection-query formation from single-frame detection and construct such queries before the decoder with little awareness of trajectory states. Consequently, currently untracked objects may be missed, while challenging tracked objects with reduced visibility under occlusion may lack complementary evidence, causing association failures or duplicate responses. To address these issues, we propose TAQ-MOTR, a tracking-aware detection query formation framework that employs a pre-decoder Hybrid Query Generator (HQG) to fuse current-frame image features, track memory, and learnable memory. By conditioning detection queries on trajectory states, TAQ-MOTR adapts them to \rev{the discovery of currently untracked objects and tracked-object complementation We further introduce a training-only auxiliary detection branch whose one-to-one label assignment is decoupled from that of the main tracking branch, providing additional detection supervision to strengthen the shared HQG and decoder for the discovery of currently untracked objects. TAQ-MOTR improves performance on DanceTrack, SportsMOT, and BFT, achieving 72.0 HOTA, 63.1 AssA, and 76.6 IDF1 on the DanceTrack test set. Code is available at https://github.com/Magicmiya/TAQ-MOTR
